proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter hypothesis. Choose an arbitrary point O and call its color c. To prove the coloring is constant, assume there exists a point G of the other color. Let r=dist(O,G)>0 and choose the small radius s=r/4, so 0<s<r/2. By the finite geometric configuration lemma, we can select five distinct auxiliary points X_1,...,X_5 on the small circle centered at G of radius s, and for each X_i two support points A_i,B_i on the large circle centered at O of radius r, with all ten support points pairwise distinct and arranged so that X_i is the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i. Because the large circle is centered at O, the circle bound lemma implies that at most two of these ten support points can have the color opposite to c. A simple pigeonhole argument then gives at least three indices i for which both A_i and B_i have color c. For each such index, the color-transfer lemma shows that X_i must also have color c, because X_i is the circumcenter of the monochromatic triangle O A_i B_i. Thus the small circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying the circle-center lemma to that circle forces G itself to have color c, contradicting the choice of G as opposite-colored. Therefore no opposite-colored point exists, so every point of the plane has color c. Since f was arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the root hypothesis: for every noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).
steps.trivial_justification: This is the assumption of the root theorem, specialized to an arbitrary coloring f.

steps.derives: Choose an arbitrary point O in R^2 and set c := f(O). To prove the theorem, it is enough to show that every point P in R^2 satisfies f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: If every point has the same color as the fixed point O, then the coloring is constant with witness color c.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that there exists a point G in R^2 with f(G) != c.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a standard contradiction setup for the universal statement proved in A2.

steps.derives: The points O and G are distinct, so r := dist(O,G) satisfies r > 0.
steps.trivial_justification: Since f(O)=c and f(G)≠c, the points O and G cannot be equal. Distinct points in the Euclidean plane have strictly positive distance, so r=dist(O,G)>0.

steps.derives: Define s := r/4. Then 0 < s < r/2.
steps.trivial_justification: From A4 we have r>0. Therefore r/4>0, and also r/4<r/2 by elementary arithmetic on positive real numbers.

steps.derives: There exist five pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 on Circle(G,s) and, for each i in {1,2,3,4,5}, two distinct support points A_i,B_i on Circle(O,r) such that dist(X_i,A_i)=dist(X_i,B_i)=dist(O,X_i), and all ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L4 to the distinct points O,G with r=dist(O,G) and the positive radius s satisfying 0<s<r/2.

steps.derives: Among the ten pairwise distinct support points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 on Circle(O,r), at most two have color different from c.
steps.trivial_justification: By A2, c=f(O). Every support point lies on Circle(O,r) by A6. Lemma L2 says that any circle centered at O contains at most two points of the color opposite to f(O)=c. Hence at most two of these ten support points have color different from c.

steps.derives: There exist at least three indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} such that both support points A_i and B_i have color c.
steps.trivial_justification: Instantiate L5 with the five labeled pairs (A_i,B_i), preferred color c, and opposite color the other element of {red,green}. Step A7 provides the hypothesis that at most two of the ten support points are not colored c.

steps.derives: For each index i produced in A8, the auxiliary point X_i has color c. Therefore there exist three distinct points among X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 lying on Circle(G,s) and colored c.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix one index i from A8. Step A6 gives O != X_i indirectly because X_i lies on Circle(G,s) with s>0 while O is not forced there, and more importantly provides the equal-distance relations dist(O,A_i)=dist(O,B_i)=r and dist(X_i,A_i)=dist(X_i,B_i)=dist(O,X_i), with A_i != B_i. Since A8 gives f(A_i)=f(B_i)=c and A2 gives f(O)=c, Lemma L3 applies and yields f(X_i)=c. Repeating this for three indices from A8 gives three distinct c-colored points on Circle(G,s); distinctness follows because the X_i were pairwise distinct in A6.

steps.derives: f(G)=c, contradicting the assumption f(G) != c.
steps.trivial_justification: The three points obtained in A9 are distinct, all lie on Circle(G,s), and all have color c. Applying L1 with center G and radius s gives f(G)=c. This contradicts A3, which asserted f(G)≠c.

steps.derives: No point G in R^2 can satisfy f(G) != c. Hence for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A10 shows that any hypothetical point of color different from c leads to a contradiction. Therefore every point of the plane must have color c.

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: The color c=f(O) chosen in A2 is a valid witness by A11.

steps.derives: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 fixed an arbitrary coloring f under the theorem hypothesis, and A12 established exactly the desired conclusion for that arbitrary f.
